> 2018-03-29 14:46 GMT+02:00 Ralph Asher <ralph...@gmail.com>:
> > OK, thanks.  In practice I will have multiple attributes per "roller
> > coaster" that will go into the ranking criteria.
>
> Note that if you can retrieve them all in a vector in a single
> get_attribute call (in the decider function) if you provide a vector
> of attribute names.
>
> > As a next question, do I
> > need to explicitly list all the sub-trajectories?  Or can I have an input
> > data.frame that has columns listing all the attributes, and one row per
> > "roller coaster" ?
>
> I'm not sure I understand. You can have a data frame listing all the
> attributes, but you need to list all the sub-trajectories in either
> case. If you are worried about the amount of code to write, given that
> the sub-trajectories are equal except for the resource to
> seize/release, you can parametrise them into a function and use lapply
> to obtain a list of trajectories (see for instance how we build
> 'bh_traffic' in [1], and how we add a lot of resources further below
> with a loop). Once you have all the sub-trajectories as a list, it is
> easy to pass them to a branch using do.call.
>
> > I'm thinking of how to make it flexible enough to
> > support many (or few) roller-coasters without needing to explicitly list
> > them all in the simmer object.
>
> In general, see the techniques used in [1]. These simulations are able
> to deal with a large number of resources and entities with similar
> trajectories with the minimum number of lines of code, with a heavy
> use of lapply and for loops to build such trajectories and simulation
> environments.
>
> BTW, as this is becoming a kind of recurring topic, I think that this
> pattern may be a good candidate for simmer.bricks. I opened an issue
> there [2] to consider this feature. Any feedback would be very
> welcome. And if you are able to build this brick for your simulation,
> it would be very welcome as a PR. ;-)
>
> Iñaki
>
> [1] https://r-simmer.org/articles/simmer-aa-5g <https://www.google.com/url?q=https%3A%2F%2Fr-simmer.org%2Farticles%2Fsimmer-aa-5g&sa=D&sntz=1&usg=AFQjCNF55v9PL-8NFBSThJJqHYpJf--Fuw>
> [2] https://github.com/r-simmer/simmer.bricks/issues/5

FYI, I've closed [2] above because I found a much better solution. Follow the link to the issue and see my last comment if you are interested.

Iñaki

> > On Thursday, March 29, 2018 at 4:08:39 AM UTC-5, Iñaki Úcar wrote:
> >>
> >> 2018-03-28 20:59 GMT+02:00 Ralph Asher <ralph....@gmail.com>:
> >> > Generically, it is possible to assign arrivals to a resource based upon
> >> > a
> >> > regularly-updated preference ranking of resources, then have the
> >> > resource
> >> > wait until it gets a batch?  To use the roller-coaster example, suppose
> >> > there were five roller coasters and an "arrival" (amusement park rider)
> >> > chooses between them based upon some preference order (e.g., a
> >> > preference
> >> > score based partially on the number of people currently waiting in the
> >> > ride,
> >> > and partially upon how far the person needs to walk, a defined value).
> >>
> >> A branch should do the trick. In the 'option' argument, you have
> >> freedom to implement your decider function based on a rank or whatever
> >> you need. Then, each subtrajectory contains a roller-coaster. What you
> >> can't do, in principle, is to rely on queue counts for that decider,
> >> because arrivals wait *in the batch*, not in the resource. You can
> >> solve this by setting some global variables:
> >>
> >> - batch option=potentially_complex_function_here,
> >>   - trajectory1
> >>     - set_global "resource1" +1
> >>     - batch
> >>     - set_global "resource1" 0
> >>     - seize "resource1"
> >>     - ...
> >>   - trajectory2
> >>     - set_global "resource2" +1
> >>     - batch
> >>     - set_global "resource2" 0
> >>     - seize "resource2"
> >>     - ...
> >>   - ...
> >>
> >> etcetera. Your globals effectively are your queue counters, and you
> >> can check them in the branch decider.
> >>
> >> Also note that, with the latest version, incrementing an attribute
> >> (global or not) can be done simply as follows:
> >>
> >> set_attribute("my_key", 1, mod="+")
> >> set_global("my_key", 1, mod="+")
> >>
> >> Iñaki

> >> > to
> >> > one of multiple discrete resources based upon a preference ranking.
> >> >
> >> > Thanks
> >> > Ralph
> >> >
> >

messages.body_plain:
Hi everybody,
I would like to define queues with different disciplines, so not just according to the FIFO discipline.
http://staff.um.edu.mt/jskl1/simweb/intro.htm
Is there a way to do it in R Simmer?
I found the LIFO rule in case of preemtion, but this can be used just in case of preemtion... I would like to have a queue with LIFO (last in first out) or random rule.
Thanks a lot in advance. Regards.

messages.body_plain:
Hi, and welcome,

El mar., 7 ago. 2018 a las 13:41, Viola Gallina
(<tatay...@gmail.com>) escribió:

>
> Hi everybody,
> I would like to define queues with different disciplines, so not just according to the FIFO discipline.
> http://staff.um.edu.mt/jskl1/simweb/intro.htm
> Is there a way to do it in R Simmer?
> I found the LIFO rule in case of preemtion, but this can be used just in case of preemtion... I would like to have a queue with LIFO (last in first out) or random rule.
> Thanks a lot in advance. Regards.

In case of preemption, the LIFO rule may be applied only to the
decision of which arrival should be kicked out from the server, not to
the queue. Currently, all queues in simmer are FIFO with priorities.

You can take advantage of priorities, though, to simulate LIFO queues.
You only need to assign an increasing priority to each new arrival:

```
library(simmer)

env <- simmer()

t <- trajectory() %>%
  set_global("prio", 1, mod="+") %>%
  set_prioritization(function()
    c(get_global(env, "prio"), NA, NA), mod="+") %>%
  seize("resource") %>%
  timeout(1) %>%
  release("resource")

env %>%
  add_resource("resource") %>%
  add_generator("dummy", t, at(rep(0, 5))) %>%
  run() %>%
  get_mon_arrivals()
#>     name start_time end_time activity_time finished replication
#> 1 dummy0          0        1             1     TRUE           1
#> 2 dummy4          0        2             1     TRUE           1
#> 3 dummy3          0        3             1     TRUE           1
#> 4 dummy2          0        4             1     TRUE           1
#> 5 dummy1          0        5             1     TRUE           1
```

As you can see, arrivals 1-4 are enqueued and served in a LIFO basis.
To simulate a random rule, it's easier: just assign random priorities.
Hope it helps.

Regards,
Iñaki

messages.body_plain:
Hi,
yes, you can do it in this way, but I think it would be easier to have an opportunity to chose other disciplines than FIFO.
If you have several resources in your system, and one or few of them can have more than one capacity and if you use clones it can be very complicated to apply your suggested solution.
By the way hier you can find the LIFO queue in Simpy: https://docs.python.org/3/library/queue.html
So in my opinion it would be great to have other queue disciplines (LIFO or random) in Simmer
Regards, Viola

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I have this problem:

You have 7 types of testers with different test times (in seconds):
T1 T2 T3 T4 T5 T6 T7
98 41 204 177 375 130 281

Each products needs to run through all the testers. The products arrive at a conveyor. The transfer time from conveyor to tester is on average 7.6s (robot). The average movement time from tester to tester is 5s.
You can group testers together in bunches of 24. Any combination of T1-T7 testers in the group is possible. The conveyor connects the different groups of testers. The transfer time between tester groups is 20s. The order in which the tests are run is important.

How many tester of each tester type would you need to optimize throughput? What should be the grouping of the testers?

And I am trying to solve it by using simmer. I defined a trajectory for the product (3 testers in this case):

env<-simmer("Optimizing throughput")
env

product<-trajectory("sample") %>%
    timeout(function() rnorm(1,0.12)) %>%
    seize("T1",1)%>%
    timeout(function() rnorm(1,1.63)) %>%
    release("T1",1)%>%

    seize("T2",1)%>%
    timeout(function() rnorm(1,0.68)) %>%
    release("T2",1)%>%

    seize("T3",1)%>%
    timeout(function() rnorm(1,3.4)) %>%
    release("T3",1)

envs<-lapply(1:100, function(i){
    simmer() %>%
        add_generator("product", product, at(seq(0,60*4,0.08))) %>%
        add_resource("T1",1) %>%
        add_resource("T2",1) %>%
        add_resource("T3",1) %>%
        run()
})

With one tester of each type, I get 3001 products served in this process with this calculation:

get_mon_arrivals(envs) %>%
    group_by(replication) %>%
    summarise(n=n()) %>%
    .$n %>% mean

And I tried to optimize by using this code:

expand.grid(nr_T1 = 1:10,
            nr_T2 = 1:10,
            nr_T3 = 1:10) %>% nrow()

library(simmer.optim)

sim_model<-function(){
    product<-trajectory("sample") %>%
        timeout(function() rnorm(1,0.12)) %>%
        seize("T1",1)%>%
        timeout(function() rnorm(1,1.63)) %>%
        release("T1",1)%>%

        seize("T2",1)%>%
        timeout(function() rnorm(1,0.68)) %>%
        release("T2",1)%>%

        seize("T3",1)%>%
        timeout(function() rnorm(1,3.4)) %>%
        release("T3",1)

    env<-simmer() %>%
        add_generator("product", product, at(seq(0,60*4,0.08))) %>%
        add_resource("T1", .opt("nr_T1")) %>%
        add_resource("T2", .opt("nr_T2")) %>%
        add_resource("T3", .opt("nr_T3"))

    env
}

set.seed(2016)
r <- simmer_optim(
    model = sim_model,
    method = grid_optim,
    direction = "max",
    objective = msr_arrivals_finished,
    constraints = list(with_args(assert_waiting_time_max, max_val=50000)),
    params = list(nr_T1 = par_discrete(1:10),
                  nr_T2 = par_discrete(1:10),
                  nr_T3 = par_discrete(1:10)
    ),
    control = optim_control(run_args = list(until=8*60)))
r

I really don't have other constraints since the testers will run 24/7 so I only added waiting time to be less than a value. And this is my output:

simmer.optim result

method:                 grid_optim
objective value:        1417
constraints satisfied:  TRUE

params:
>  nr_T1 :  9
>  nr_T2 :  3
>  nr_T3 :  10

As I understand, I have produced 1417 products, if I increase the number of testers by the quantities given by the optimization function. Is this correct? If I change my trajectory to include these quantities by tester I still get the same 3001 products I originally calculated... Could you please advise? Any suggestions would be greatly appreciated!

Thanks,

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm having some trouble using get_global() within set_source(). The idea is that the arrival time should depend upon a global attribute (in this case "hazard ratio") being set by other trajectories within the model. In this particular instance, I actually only need the number the once - the simulation effectively terminates after this arrival (or rather, I throw out all data produced after it during post-processing), so I don't even need the attribute value at any time other than when setting the generator. My current code is this:

 set_source("standard_mortality", function() rexp(1, get_global(env, "hazard_ratio") / 2048)) %>%
 log_("debugging") %>%
 activate("standard_mortality")

(with some surrounding trajectory stuff setting other generators and attributes).

The error message is "Error: 'standard_mortality' at 2.00: Evaluation error: there is no arrival running.". The log_() runs fine, so  my interpretation is that set_source() does exactly what it is supposed to, and sets the generator to generate arrivals at a rate function() rexp(1, get_global(env, "hazard_ratio") / 2048) - the problem (I think) is that when the generator fires up, it is calling get_global outside of a trajectory.

Is my understanding right? Is there a solution? I wondered if a standard-R variable work better than attributes in this case, but even if it would work, it didn't feel like a particularly elegant solution.

Many thanks,
Jacob

Your understanding is right, and a standard R variable is the solution.

Currently, set/get_global is just a shortcut for set/get_attribute
with a "global" parameter set to true, which means that an arrival is
queried to get the value. As you said, when the generator fires up,
there's no arrival running: the generator is running.

I'm planning to change that, because you are not the first one to
expect this (i.e., calling get_global from a generator) to work. As
you can see in [1], I'm planning to implement add_global, at the same
level as add_generator or add_resource, to easily set up global
variables at the beginning of a simulation (schedules will be allowed
too). This will give global variables their own "status", which will
allow me to unlink them from attributes.

Then, get_global won't be just a shortcut and should work in a
generator. This requires some work, so you should expect a couple of
releases until this is available.

My example below - the variable I am modifying is idx:

idx <- 0
setBatch <- function(){
  idx <- idx + 1
  return(0)
}

And then within the trajectory I call the timeout before indexing the vector for my set_source call:

trj %>% timeout(function() setBatch()) %>% set_source('gallon_', batch_speeds[idx])

Hope this helps,
John
